group.title: Arts and culture
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A set of ideas about beauty and style that guides an artist or a movement.
examples: The film’s dreamy {aesthetic} owes much to old painting.
wrong: The aesthetic of the building had nothing to do with how it looked.

words.meaning: A person who chooses and looks after the objects in a museum or exhibition.
examples: The {curator} selected forty paintings for the show.
wrong: The curator has no say in which works the museum displays.

words.meaning: To select and arrange works or items for people to see or use.
examples: She {curated} an exhibition of young African photographers.
wrong: He curated the show by hanging random pieces without any plan.

words.meaning: A careful written or spoken judgment of a work, idea or performance.
examples: Her {critique} of the novel praised its style but not its plot.
wrong: The critique gave no judgment of the play at all.

words.meaning: Publicly praised by many people, especially critics.
examples: The {acclaimed} director won three major awards.
wrong: The acclaimed novel was ignored or attacked by every critic.

words.meaning: New and experimental, especially in art, music or writing.
examples: The gallery shows {avant-garde} work that challenges traditional ideas.
wrong: His avant-garde music sounded exactly like every traditional folk song.

words.meaning: Using shapes, colors and lines rather than showing real people or things.
examples: The {abstract} painting is just bold red squares on a white background.
wrong: The abstract portrait looked exactly like a photograph of the man.

words.meaning: Showing people, animals or objects in a way that looks like the real world.
examples: She prefers {figurative} painting to purely abstract art.
wrong: The figurative sculpture showed no recognizable shape at all.

words.meaning: The way someone or something is shown in art, film or writing.
examples: The film’s {portrayal} of the king is surprisingly sympathetic.
wrong: Her portrayal of the queen was a speech she never performed or wrote.

words.meaning: To show someone or something in a picture, story or film.
examples: The mural {depicts} the history of the town.
wrong: The painting depicts a ship, though nothing at all appears in it.

words.meaning: The material or method an artist uses, such as oil paint, clay or film.
examples: Watercolor is a difficult {medium} to master.
wrong: The artist’s medium is the price of her paintings.

words.meaning: A large artwork made for a specific space, often filling a whole room.
examples: The {installation} filled the hall with hanging glass lights.
wrong: The installation was a tiny drawing in a small frame.

words.meaning: An exhibition that shows an artist’s work from across their whole career.
examples: The museum is holding a {retrospective} of her fifty years of painting.
wrong: The retrospective only showed paintings she finished last week.

words.meaning: A person who gives money or support to artists or arts organizations.
examples: A wealthy {patron} paid for the new concert hall.
wrong: The patron refused to give the orchestra any support.

words.meaning: To formally ask an artist to create a particular work, and pay for it.
examples: The city {commissioned} a statue for the new square.
wrong: They commissioned the portrait by refusing to pay the artist anything.

words.meaning: Famous and admired for a particular skill or achievement.
examples: The concert features a {renowned} cellist.
wrong: The renowned singer is completely unknown outside her family.

words.meaning: A person with outstanding skill, especially in playing music.
examples: The young violin {virtuoso} played without a single mistake.
wrong: The virtuoso could barely play a simple tune.

words.meaning: All the pieces that a performer or company is ready to perform.
examples: The pianist has a wide {repertoire}, from Bach to jazz.
wrong: Her repertoire includes songs she has never learned.

words.meaning: The planning and arrangement of steps and movements in a dance.
examples: The {choreography} blends ballet with street dance.
wrong: The choreography was the music the orchestra played.

words.meaning: A particular performance of a song, piece of music or role.
examples: She gave a moving {rendition} of the old folk song.
wrong: His rendition of the song was never performed by anyone.

words.meaning: A particular way of understanding or performing a work of art.
examples: The director’s {interpretation} sets the play in modern times.
wrong: Every reader has the same interpretation, so the novel has no other meanings.

words.meaning: The use of objects, colors or images to stand for ideas.
examples: The novel is full of {symbolism}; the storm represents the hero’s anger.
wrong: The symbolism showed that nothing in the poem stood for anything else.

words.meaning: An image, idea or pattern that appears again and again in a work.
examples: Water is a recurring {motif} in her paintings.
wrong: The motif appears only once and is never repeated.

words.meaning: Bringing strong images, memories or feelings to mind.
examples: The {evocative} music took me straight back to my childhood.
wrong: The evocative poem stirred no feelings or memories in anyone.

words.meaning: Causing a strong feeling of sadness or sympathy.
examples: The final scene, where the father says goodbye, is deeply {poignant}.
wrong: The poignant ending made everyone laugh without a care.

words.meaning: Intellectual and serious, and usually enjoyed by educated people.
examples: The station plays {highbrow} classical music and poetry readings.
wrong: The highbrow show was full of silly slapstick jokes.

words.meaning: Simple and popular, and not intended to be intellectual.
examples: He enjoys {lowbrow} comedies as much as serious drama.
wrong: The lowbrow lecture was a dense philosophical analysis.

words.meaning: Liked or accepted by most people; not unusual or extreme.
examples: The band moved from small clubs into {mainstream} success.
wrong: Her mainstream music is known by only a handful of fans.

words.meaning: Appealing to a small, specialized group of people.
examples: The shop sells {niche} records for serious collectors.
wrong: The niche film was a hit with almost everyone in the country.

words.meaning: A person who does not understand or value art and culture.
examples: Only a {philistine} would turn that old theater into a parking lot.
wrong: The philistine spent every weekend at galleries and the opera.

words.meaning: An expert who has great knowledge and good judgment about art, food or wine.
examples: A {connoisseur} of jazz, he can name the player after a few notes.
wrong: As a wine connoisseur, she can’t tell red from white.

words.meaning: Art or objects thought to be cheap, showy and in poor taste, sometimes enjoyed ironically.
examples: The shop is full of {kitsch}, like glittery plastic swans.
wrong: The kitsch was elegant and admired for its refined taste.

words.meaning: Trying to seem more important, clever or artistic than you really are.
examples: The film was so {pretentious} that the dialogue was almost unbearable.
wrong: His pretentious style was plain, modest and simple.

words.meaning: Copying other people’s work too closely; not original.
examples: Critics called the album {derivative} of 1970s rock.
wrong: The derivative novel was praised as the most original book of the year.

words.meaning: Using very few simple shapes, colors or elements on purpose.
examples: The gallery’s white walls suit her {minimalist} sculptures.
wrong: The minimalist painting was crowded with hundreds of bright details.

words.meaning: Attractive and chosen with good judgment about style.
examples: The room was decorated in a {tasteful}, simple style.
wrong: The tasteful outfit was loud, clashing and over the top.

words.meaning: The group of works generally accepted as the most important in a field.
examples: Her novels are now part of the literary {canon}.
wrong: The canon includes only books that critics have forgotten.

words.meaning: Very famous and widely seen as a symbol of something.
examples: The {iconic} photo of the moon landing is known worldwide.
wrong: The iconic image is one that nobody remembers.

words.meaning: Using humor and exaggeration to criticize people or ideas, especially in politics.
examples: The show uses {satire} to mock powerful politicians.
wrong: The satire praised the government seriously, without any humor.

words.meaning: A funny imitation of a work or style that exaggerates it.
examples: The film is a {parody} of old spy movies.
wrong: The parody was a serious, exact copy with no humor.
